<reason>Both sides were sharp and adaptive, and CON deserves credit for the two most original moves in the debate: the indeterminacy attack on "genuinely necessary," and the inversion of the equity case (the diploma as the one portable, publicly verifiable asset a networkless applicant can earn alone). CON also handled PRO's Q1 well by explaining why electrician/driver/cashier postings are easy cases (licensing substitutes, cheap error) while the supervisor posting is not. But CON's two load-bearing claims each took clean damage. First, the substitution harm: PRO showed that interviews and referrals already operate on top of the degree filter, so removing gate one does not create gate two, and "losing at gate one is not fairer than competing at gate two." Second, and decisively, CON repeatedly framed the motion as "stripping" the credential, when the motion only removes the requirement — PRO named this precisely ("her diploma still speaks for her... nobody loses a credential, someone gains a hearing"), and CON never squarely answered it, which hollows out its strongest equity line. CON's gesture-or-override dilemma was the best pressure of the debate, and PRO's answer (a practice norm, like "don't ask applicants their age," whose work is forcing the question nobody currently asks; and that the natural experiment shows wording changed while screening didn't, which the motion targets) was adequate rather than crushing. Meanwhile PRO's turn of CON's own natural-experiment evidence left CON's predicted quality/chaos harm speculative, and CON never weighed odds-shifting value against the cost of discarding most of the labor market. PRO's execution costs are real — three clipped turns and two miscited reference IDs (C-prefixed) — which keeps this from being a solid win rather than a narrow one.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's handling of CON's "the degree is the only credential a stranger with no network can earn alone": PRO pointed out the sentence excludes the stranger with no network *and* no money, and that under the motion the graduate keeps her diploma's signal entirely — she loses only the exclusivity of the gate. CON's reply ("a scholarship exists; a network does not go on sale") was memorable but did not repair the misdescription of "stop requiring" as "strip the credential," leaving CON's central equity inversion damaged.</best_rebuttal>
